hook_text: Six squares can be arranged in dozens of ways. Only eleven fold into a box. Two quick tests spot the fakes.
clip_script: Cut open a cube box and lay it flat. That shape is a net. Every cube net is six squares, but most six-square shapes are fakes. Test one: a row of five squares in a line. Fake. Four squares already wrap all the way round, so the fifth lands on top of the first. Test two: a two by two block. Fake. That would put four faces at one corner, and a cube corner only ever has three. The famous cross passes: a row of four, one square up, one square down. Want to number it as a die? In any straight line of three squares, the first and third end up opposite. Opposite faces on a die add to seven: one and six, two and five, three and four. Fill them in and fold. Eleven real nets, two tests, and opposites that make seven.
visual_style: Paper squares slide into arrangements on a whiteboard; a row of five flashes red and folds over itself; a two by two block flashes red; the cross folds up neatly into a cube while numbers appear on opposite pairs.
pacing: Quick setup, a snap on each fake, a satisfying fold at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for nets of prisms, pyramids and cylinders, and how to build your own models.
